pluss::timeline::time¶

Back to Timeline Factory API Reference

Signatures¶

Timeline pluss::timeline::time(std::string_view value)
Timeline pluss::timeline::time(string_range values)
Timeline pluss::timeline::time(nested_string_values values)
Timeline pluss::timeline::time(string_range flat, integer_range sizes)

Turn Clock Readings Into Comparable Instants¶

time() accepts clock-only text and anchors it to 1970-01-01. A Timeline always stores instants, so this anchor gives clock readings a stable numeric representation without pretending they recur every day. Use time() for time-of-day values that need ordering, duration arithmetic, shape, or exact nanosecond storage. Use make() when a real calendar date is present.

The default anchor timezone is UTC. A numeric offset on the clock is accepted and identifies an instant relative to that UTC anchor. For example, 09:30:00-07:00 becomes 16:30:00Z. This may be useful for protocol fields, but a named civil timezone and its daylight-saving rules require an actual date; an isolated clock cannot determine which seasonal offset applies.

Accepted clocks are HH:MM or HH:MM:SS, optionally followed by fractional seconds and a numeric offset. Hours are 0..23, minutes and seconds are 0..59, and leap-second spelling 60 is rejected. Fractions are retained to nanosecond precision.

Example 1: One Nanosecond After The Anchor¶

const auto tick = pluss::timeline::time("00:00:00.000000001");
std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::timeline::format(tick, "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000001+00:00"

The scalar has shape []. The explicit formatter is used because the compact Timeline printer does not expose fractional nanoseconds.

Example 2: Minute And Fractional Forms¶

const auto clocks = pluss::timeline::time({"09:30", "17:45:30.250"});
std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::timeline::format(clocks, "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["1970-01-01T09:30:00.000000000+00:00", "1970-01-01T17:45:30.250000000+00:00"]

Omitted seconds become zero. A three-digit fraction means 250 milliseconds, which occupies the first three of nine fractional digits.

Example 3: Numeric Offset Normalization¶

const auto clock = pluss::timeline::time("09:30:00-07:00");
std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::timeline::format(clock, "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"1970-01-01T16:30:00.000000000+00:00"

The source offset is consumed to determine the instant; it is not retained as display metadata.

Example 4: Explicit Matrix Shape¶

const std::vector<std::string> flat{
    "00:00:00", "06:00:00", "12:00:00", "18:00:00"};
const auto matrix = pluss::timeline::time(flat, {2, 2});
std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::timeline::format(matrix, "%FT%T.%f%z")) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2, 2], dim=2, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
[
  ["1970-01-01T00:00:00.000000000+00:00", "1970-01-01T06:00:00.000000000+00:00"], 
  ["1970-01-01T12:00:00.000000000+00:00", "1970-01-01T18:00:00.000000000+00:00"]
]

Nested braces can infer the same shape. Flat-plus-shape is preferable when the values and geometry arrive separately at runtime.

Validation And Failure¶

Dates, empty tokens, impossible clock fields, invalid offsets, ragged nesting, shape mismatches, and ranks above three throw. No wrapping is performed: 24:00:00 does not become the following day, and 23:59:60 does not become midnight.

try {
  (void)pluss::timeline::time("23:59:60");
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "rejected\n";
}

Output¶

rejected
